sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in St. Paul?
sections.html:
St. Paul adds a step that most Minnesota cities lack: a city-licensed evaluator must inspect most one- and two-unit homes before the listing goes live. The city calls it Truth-in-Sale of Housing, or TISH, and it applies to single-family houses, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes.

The rest of the process looks like a sale anywhere in the state. You sign a disclosure, record a deed in Ramsey County and settle taxes at closing. Your route (agent listing, owner sale or a direct cash offer) changes the timeline more than the paperwork. The sections below cover the St. Paul rules first, then the neighborhood and housing facts that shape pricing.

sections.h2: What does St. Paul look like by the numbers?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimates 306,684 people lived in St. Paul on July 1, 2025. That is 1.5% fewer than the 311,503 April 2020 base, so the capital city shrank slightly while Woodbury and Sherburne County grew.

  • 125,249 households averaging 2.37 people (2020 to 2024)
  • 52.9% of homes owner-occupied, so nearly half of the housing stock is rented
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $294,500
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,911
  • Median gross rent: $1,281
  • Median household income: $73,394, with 43.8% of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree

Those figures explain why many St. Paul sellers hold rental or inherited property. A house that sat as a rental for years often has deferred repairs, and the TISH report will record them for buyers.

sections.h2: Who needs a Truth-in-Sale of Housing report, and when?
sections.html:
Owners of single-family homes, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes need a TISH evaluation before the home is marketed for sale. Buildings with three or more units, commercial buildings and mixed-use buildings are outside the program. A condominium with its own Ramsey County parcel number still needs a report even when the building holds a certificate of occupancy, because that certificate only covers common areas.

The report must be available to any prospective buyer within three calendar days of listing. It stays good for 365 days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If your offer is accepted inside that year, closing can fall after the expiration date without a new report.

The evaluator is a private contractor licensed by the city, and the evaluator sets the fee. The city does not recommend anyone. Call the Department of Safety and Inspections at 651-266-8989 before you list if you are unsure whether your sale needs a report.

sections.h2: What does the TISH report actually require me to fix?
sections.html:
Very little. The report is disclosure only, and the single mandatory item in a single-family house is a working hard-wired smoke alarm. If the evaluator marks it as a hazard, the city's electrical inspector sends a letter and you must hire a licensed electrical contractor to pull a permit and install the alarm. The contractor then calls the inspector to close the permit.

Everything else on the report informs the buyer and does not force a repair. Sellers who want to avoid hazard marks can fix items first, and the city publishes a list of the ten most common deficiencies for that purpose. Failing to follow the program is a misdemeanor under Chapter 189 of the Saint Paul Legislative Code.

sections.h2: Which sales are exempt from TISH?
sections.html:
The table lists the main rules from the city's Truth-in-Sale of Housing page.

Truth-in-Sale of Housing rules, as listed on the City of Saint Paul Safety and Inspections page
QuestionAnswer
Covered propertiesSingle-family, duplex, condominium, townhome
Not coveredThree or more units, commercial, mixed-use
Deadline to have report on handWithin three calendar days of listing

Aunts, uncles and cousins do not count as immediate family under the program. The same page requires a smoking policy disclosure form when you sell a unit in a condominium, townhome or similar community, a rule that took effect January 1, 2022.

sections.h2: How do St. Paul's rent rules affect a rental house I want to sell?
sections.html:
They matter to your buyer more than to you, but they affect what the property is worth. Voters approved a rent stabilization ordinance on November 2, 2021, and the City Council amended it in September 2022 and May 2025. Rent increases are capped at 3% in a 12-month period unless an exception applies.

  • Self-certification: available for increases from 3% to 8%, evaluated each year
  • Just cause vacancy: the consumer price index change plus 8%, after city review
  • Staff determination: no fixed limit when the landlord justifies the figure
  • Separate tracks exist for new construction and for low-income housing providers

A tenant-occupied house therefore comes with limits on how fast the next owner can raise the rent. Vacant houses give a buyer more room, which is one reason investors look at emptied rentals. If tenants live in the home, ask the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 how the rules apply to your unit.

sections.h2: What shapes the housing stock across St. Paul?
sections.html:
Water and hills explain most of the map. The city grew at the junction of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers, on bluffs the glaciers cut, and it covers 56.18 square miles, of which 51.98 are land. The city planning office divides the area into 17 planning districts, and each has a council that weighs in on land use.

Older neighborhoods near downtown and along the river carry homes from the steamboat and railroad eras. The 1904 storms that damaged hundreds of downtown buildings and the 1960s freeway work, which cleared the Rondo neighborhood for Interstate 94, both left marks on where houses stand today. On the south side, the former Ford assembly plant site in Highland Park is being redeveloped as Highland Bridge, planned with about 3,800 housing units.

Winters are cold and snowy, and the city expects more spring and summer rain over time, which can lead to river and flash flooding. Buyers and inspectors in St. Paul look hard at basements, roofs and drainage for that reason.

sections.h2: How do transit, schools and parks affect a St. Paul sale?
sections.html:
Getting around is easy by Twin Cities standards. Interstates 94 and 35E cross the city, along with US 52 and Minnesota 280 and 5. The METRO Green Line runs along University Avenue to Minneapolis, the A Line serves arterial streets, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops at Union Depot.

The city runs 160 parks and 41 recreation centers, and a 2018 ranking placed its park access second nationally behind Minneapolis. Saint Paul Public Schools is the state's largest district, and families can also use charter schools, private schools and open enrollment. Macalester College, the University of St. Thomas, Hamline University and Saint Catherine University all sit within the city, which keeps demand steady for houses near campuses.

sections.h2: What closing steps apply to a St. Paul house sale?
sections.html:
Minnesota requires a written disclosure of material facts about the property before you sign a sale agreement, under Minnesota Statutes 513.55. The disclosure must be made in good faith and reflect what you know.

The deed gets recorded where the property sits, which for St. Paul is Ramsey County. Ask the Ramsey County recorder for current recording fees and ask your title company who files the paperwork. Keep your TISH report, any smoke alarm permit and repair receipts together so your closing agent can pass copies to the buyer.

A direct sale to a cash buyer changes the schedule but the city rules above still apply to the property. Ask Safety and Inspections whether a report is needed before you accept an offer.

faqs.q: Do I need a TISH report to sell my St. Paul house?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is a single-family home, duplex, condominium or townhome and the sale is not to immediate family. Buildings with three or more units are exempt. The report must be on hand within three calendar days of listing.

faqs.q: How long is a TISH report valid?
faqs.a: It is valid for 365 consecutive days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If a seller accepts an offer within that year, closing may fall afterward without a new report.

faqs.q: What is the one repair TISH can force?
faqs.a: A working hard-wired smoke alarm in single-family homes. If one is missing or not working, the city sends a letter and a licensed electrician must install one under a permit.

faqs.q: Does Ramsey County or the city record my deed?
faqs.a: Ramsey County records deeds for St. Paul property. The city handles the TISH report, rental rules and permits, so you deal with two offices during a sale.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with tenants in St. Paul?
faqs.a: Yes. Existing leases continue under the rent stabilization rules, which cap increases at 3% a year unless an exception is granted. Call the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 for questions about your unit.
